summary: A 1970 note by Steve Crocker on third-level ideas for the Network Information Center (NIC), and other miscellaneous thoughts. It was updated by RFC 80 and RFC 93 and replaced by RFC 123.

eli5.summary: A note of ideas for how people could look up information on the network. A newer note replaced it.

questions: how did the arpanet dial-up protocol work
what was the arpanet standard console
subtitle: Notes from a 1970 meeting on how to reach a remote host's logger and a standard network console.

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET sites needed an agreed way for a process at one host to get in touch with the logger at another host, and a common idea of what a console looks like.
tldr.mechanism: A dial-up protocol has the using host request a connection to socket 1 on the serving host, which replies with an even 32-bit socket number SS; SS and SS+1 are then used for the contact. A standard console is 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit fields.
tldr.outcome: The RFC's status is listed as Unknown. It was updated by RFC 80 and RFC 93 and replaced by RFC 123.

sections.title: The 12 August 1970 Meeting
sections.content: Steve Crocker of UCLA wrote this note on 26 August 1970. It reports that on 12 August 1970 he met people from BBN and MIT, and that they discussed the third-level protocol. The note records two things agreed at the meeting: a dial-up protocol and a standard console.
sections.eli5: A few people met to agree on how computers should say hello, and this note writes down what they decided.

sections.title: The Dial-Up Protocol
sections.content:
The aim is to put a process at the using site in contact with the logger at the serving site. The using process attaches a receive socket US and asks for a connection to socket 1 at the serving host. Its NCP sends an RTS and an ALL message over link 1.

The serving host may refuse with the standard CLS. If it accepts, it sends exactly an even 32-bit number over the connection and closes it. That number, SS, names a receive socket in the serving host. This socket and the next higher one are reserved for contact with the user.

Both NCPs then exchange CLS, STR and RTS messages on sockets SS, SS+1, US and US+1. At that point the user should be connected to the logger at the serving site.
sections.eli5: One computer knocks on door 1. If the other agrees, it hands back an even number meaning a new pair of doors, and they talk through those instead.

sections.title: The Standard Console
sections.content:
The meeting also agreed an initial network standard console: 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit fields with the eighth bit on, sent in contiguous streams. The specific codes are in appendix H of the IMP Operations manual, BBN report #1877. The note says this works only some hardship on PDP-10s and is fine for all others.

For break or interrupt, many systems use one of the standard characters. For systems that need another kind of signal, an INR message sent over the control link should suffice.
sections.eli5: Everyone agreed how a keyboard and screen should look to the network, so any computer could use any other's.

messages.label: RTS (socket 1)
messages.note: Asks for contact from receive socket US.

messages.label: STR, then SS
messages.note: Sends an even 32-bit socket number, then closes.

messages.label: CLS, STR, RTS
messages.note: Sets up connections on SS and SS+1.
